Thank you for submitting your article "A team of heterochromatin factors collaborates with small RNA pathways to combat repetitive elements and germline stress" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Jessica Tyler (Senior Editor) and three reviewers, one of whom, Edith Heard (Reviewer #1), is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

In this paper, McMurchy, Stempor et al., investigate the relationship between repetitive elements and heterochromatin and the interaction between heterochromatin factors and small RNA pathways in C. elegans. They systematically investigate a series of five heterochromatin factors (HPL-2/HP1, LIN-13, MBT-repeat protein LIN-61, LET-418/Mi-2, and the H3K9me2 histone methyltransferase MET-2/SETDB1) that have fertility phenotypes when mutated, for their binding profiles and for their impact on repeat elements, DNA repair and apoptosis in the germ line. Their results show that these heterochromatin proteins repress the expression (and potentially the noncoding activity – recombination) of repetitive DNA elements in C. elegans germ cells. They also investigate the relationships between these heterochromatin factors and the piRNA and nuclear RNAi pathways. Their study reveals that heterochromatin proteins and small RNA pathways display overlapping as well as unique control of repetitive elements in the germ line.

This work brings several important new insights:

It provides solid genetic and functional links between key factors previously shown to be associated with heterochromatin and known to lead to sterility when mutated.

It demonstrates that derepression of repetitive elements in heterochromatin mutants is one of the reasons these mutants are sterile.

It describes the genomic co-localisation of these five heterochromatin factors, particularly at repetitive elements associated with H3K9 methylation.

It provides new insights into the role that binding of these heterochromatin factors has at repeats, as RNA-seq revealed that although most repeats are derepressed to a small extent, the most affected repetitive elements in heterochromatin mutants were those encoding for transposases – these being the most critical for protection of the germ line from repeat reactivation.

It provides a convincing demonstration that repeat element upregulation is a contributing factor to infertility in heterochromatin mutants by using RNAi knockdown of the repetitive element MIRAGE1 which rescues sterility.

It demonstrates that the piRNA pathway is impeded upon loss of heterochromatin factors by demonstrating the derepression of a piRNA sensor in heterochromatin mutants.

It also shows that the nuclear RNAi pathway is largely independent of the heterochromatin and piRNA pathways, as a very different spectrum of repetitive element derepression was found in nrde-2 mutants compared to the prg-1 piRNA mutant or heterochromatin mutants.

It allows the conclusion, from genetic tests, that these alternate pathways are acting redundantly at some repeats, and uniquely at others.

Overall this is an elegant study, combining genetic and genomic approaches to investigate the role that heterochromatin factors play in repetitive element germ line control and fertility in C. elegans. It provides novel mechanistic insights into the multiple levels at which heterochromatin factors can act, not only in silencing repeats but also participating in DNA repair pathways to maintain genome integrity. The experiments are extremely well conducted, clearly presented and discussed. The interactions between heterochromatin factor pathways and small RNA pathways are still rather tenuous and could be further explored as suggested below.

Essential points:

1) Does upregulation of repetitive elements through loss of heterochromatin disable or overload the piRNA pathway? The authors could address this by small RNA-seq in the different heterochromatin mutant backgrounds, and would expect to see a change in the 21U/22G population if the piRNA pathway is overloaded (i.e. upregulation of a repetitive element leads to a bias in the 22G population in the mutant and a decrease in other 22Gs), or a loss of 21Us if piRNAs are completely eliminated. A simpler experiment might be to see whether any of the RNAi treatments in Figure 4 restore piRNA sensor silencing in the heterochromatin factor mutant backgrounds to link repetitive element expression and/or DNA repair to piRNA pathway function.

2) The authors could use ChIP-seq or immunofluorescence for histone modifications in heterochromatin factor mutant backgrounds in order to demonstrate the loss of heterochromatin marks at repetitive elements. Without such experiments, the connection between heterochromatin proteins and small RNA pathways remains tenuous. If the authors cannot add such experiments they must at least explain and discuss this.

3) In Figure 4: Is the increase in fertility in response to mirage, cep-1, and spo-11 knockdown (KD) a general phenomenon or specific to heterochromatin mutants? The authors could compare the brood size of wt cells with and without KD of the above genes. Measure fold change in wt plus or minus KD and compare to the fold change seen in mutants.

4) Figure 5: how specific is the cep-1-mediated promotion of apoptosis in response to DNA damage? Do cells with no DDR also show an increase in survival if cep-1 is knocked down? The authors could compare the survival of wt cells with and without cep-1 knockdown and compare this to the fold change observed in mutants.

5) The authors should highlight the novelty of their own findings in this manuscript by discussing their contributions in the context of what has been previously published in nuclear RNAi, piRNA and heterochromatin in C. elegans and other organisms e.g. Ashe et al. 2012; Gu et al. 2012; Burton et al. 2011; Buckley et al. 2012; Ni et al. 2014).

results.result: All pairs of heterochromatin factors (hpl-2, lin-13, lin-61, let-418, and met-2) show genetic interactions in fertility, with double mutants displaying synthetic sterility or enhanced fertility defects compared to single mutants. This indicates that these five factors have unique and partially redundant germ line roles and may cooperate in processes required for fertility.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C2, C79, and C80 are well-supported by genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 1, including both RNAi knockdown and double mutant analyses. The systematic testing of all pairwise combinations and statistical analysis using appropriate models provides strong evidence for functional redundancy among these factors.

results.result: HPL-2, LET-418, LIN-13, LIN-61, and MET-2 show extensive co-binding genome-wide, with enrichment on distal arm regions of autosomes and strong association with repetitive elements. The five factors show high correlation with H3K9me2 but not H3K9me3, with 58% of binding sites bound by more than one factor and the largest class containing all five factors (All5).
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C39 are supported by comprehensive ChIP-seq analyses with biological replicates shown in Figure 2. The correlation analyses, peak calling with IDR methodology, and enrichment calculations are appropriately conducted. The distinction between H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 associations is particularly well-documented.

results.result: Repetitive elements are upregulated in all five heterochromatin mutants (hpl-2, let-418, lin-13, lin-61, and met-2 set-25), with 71 individual elements from 29 families derepressed. Seven MIRAGE1 DNA transposable elements are upregulated in all five mutants, and upregulated elements are highly enriched for transposase-containing elements (83-fold) and LTR retrotransposons (10-fold).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44, C47-C48, and C81 are supported by RNA-seq differential expression analyses with biological replicates. The enrichment calculations for transposase and LTR elements are appropriately conducted. Validation using uniquely mapping reads (61/71 elements confirmed) strengthens the findings. The overlap analysis showing 41% of elements upregulated in multiple mutants is well-documented.

results.result: MIRAGE1 RNA is abundant in the germ line of hpl-2, let-418, and lin-13 mutants but not in wild-type, and RNAi knockdown of MIRAGE1 partially restores fertility of these mutants. This demonstrates that inappropriate MIRAGE1 expression contributes to sterility and that heterochromatin proteins promote germ line function through repression of repetitive elements encoding transposases.
results.evaluation: Claims C45, C46, C5, and C82 are supported by RNA-FISH experiments (Figure 3E) and RNAi rescue experiments (Figure 4A). The RNAi experiments used two independent sets of clones targeting different MIRAGE1 elements, with appropriate statistical testing showing significant but modest increases in fertility. The tissue-specific expression pattern strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Heterochromatin mutants display DNA repair defects and increased germ line apoptosis. hpl-2 mutants show increased oocyte fragmentation and hypersensitivity to phospho-CHK-1 induction following ionizing radiation, while hpl-2, lin-13, lin-61, and met-2 set-25 mutants all show increased germ line apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 and C96 are supported by multiple assays including oocyte fragmentation analysis, phospho-CHK-1 staining, and CED-1::GFP apoptosis reporter experiments (Figures 5 and 5—figure supplement 1). Statistical analyses using appropriate tests (Mann-Whitney, proportions Z test) support the conclusions. The inference in C96 is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Loss of cep-1/p53 partially suppresses sterility and slow growth phenotypes of heterochromatin mutants. Both RNAi and genetic mutation of cep-1 increase fertility of hpl-2, lin-13, and let-418 mutants, suggesting that genotoxic stress and DNA damage signaling activate p53, contributing to sterility and slow growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57, C3, and C83 are supported by both RNAi experiments and double mutant analyses (Figure 4). The use of both approaches strengthens the conclusions. Statistical testing is appropriate, and the partial rescue (not complete restoration to wild-type) is appropriately noted. The inference about p53 activation (C83) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Inhibiting endogenous meiotic double strand breaks by RNAi of spo-11 increases fertility of hpl-2, lin-13, and let-418 mutants, suggesting that defects in repair of meiotic DSBs contribute to sterility of heterochromatin mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C58, C4, and C84 are supported by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 4A with appropriate statistical testing. The partial rescue is consistent with the cep-1 and MIRAGE1 results, supporting a model where multiple sources of genotoxic stress contribute to sterility. The inference in C84 is reasonable.

results.result: The piRNA pathway and heterochromatin factors have shared targets and phenotypes. Eighteen repetitive elements are upregulated in prg-1 mutants, 14 of which overlap with heterochromatin mutants including MIRAGE1 elements. prg-1 mutants show increased MIRAGE1 RNA and significantly increased germ cell death, suggesting collaboration in maintaining genomic integrity.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61 and C85 are supported by RNA-seq, RNA-FISH, and apoptosis assays (Figure 6A-B, Figure 3E). The overlap analysis is appropriately conducted, and the apoptosis measurements use the same CED-1::GFP reporter as for heterochromatin mutants, allowing direct comparison. The inference about collaboration (C85) is reasonable given the shared targets and phenotypes.

results.result: lin-61, let-418, set-25, and met-2 (weakly) are important for piRNA pathway function as assessed by desilencing of a piRNA sensor reporter, while lin-13 mutants do not show significant desilencing. This extends previous findings for hpl-2 and set-25 to additional heterochromatin factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 and C87 are supported by piRNA sensor expression assays (Figure 6C-D) with appropriate statistical testing (Fisher's exact tests) and sufficient sample sizes (minimum 100 worms per strain across four experiments). The lack of desilencing in lin-13 is appropriately noted, though the authors acknowledge this could be due to the allele being non-null.

results.result: hpl-2 mutants make normal levels of piRNAs and 22G RNAs mapping near predicted piRNA target sites, indicating that hpl-2's role in the piRNA pathway is downstream of piRNA and subsequent 22G RNA synthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C65, C66, and C86 are supported by small RNA analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) using published datasets with appropriate subsampling and analysis methods. The conclusion that hpl-2 acts downstream is a reasonable inference, though it would be strengthened by analysis of other heterochromatin factors.

results.result: nrde-2 mutants show a larger and different spectrum of repetitive element desilencing compared to prg-1 or heterochromatin mutants. Of 71 elements desilenced in nrde-2, only seven overlap with heterochromatin mutants, and MIRAGE1 elements are not desilenced. Retrotransposons are highly enriched among nrde-2 targets (45/71) whereas heterochromatin factors preferentially regulate DNA transposons.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 are supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 1 and 2). The distinct target spectra between nrde-2 and heterochromatin mutants are well-documented, with appropriate overlap analyses and repeat class distribution comparisons.

results.result: NRDE-2 and LET-418 have unique and redundant roles in repetitive element repression. nrde-2; let-418 double mutants show significantly reduced brood size and increased embryo lethality compared to single mutants, with more repeats upregulated (mostly retrotransposons) than in either single mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 and C89 are supported by double mutant brood size, embryo lethality, and RNA-seq analyses (Figure 7A-C). Statistical testing using Mann-Whitney U tests is appropriate. The genetic interaction is specific to let-418 (not observed with hpl-2 or lin-61), and the RNA-seq data showing additional derepressed elements in the double mutant provides strong evidence for redundancy.

results.result: The germ line nuclear RNAi pathway partially controls H3K9me3 levels at loci regulated by heterochromatin factors and nrde-2. Genes and repeats upregulated in nrde-2 mutants show reduced H3K9me3 in germ line nrde mutants (hrde-1, nrde-4) but not soma-specific nrde-3. However, the reduction in H3K9me3 at heterochromatin-regulated loci in nrde mutants is not sufficient for derepression.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78, C90-C91 are supported by analysis of published H3K9me3 ChIP-seq datasets in multiple nrde mutants (Figure 7—figure supplements 2 and 3). The use of appropriate statistical tests (Mann-Whitney U) and control repeat sets strengthens the analysis. The inference that H3K9me3 reduction is insufficient for derepression (C91) is well-supported by the observation that elements are not upregulated despite reduced H3K9me3.

results.result: Heterochromatin mutants show upregulation of 267-513 genes per strain, with high overlap among mutants (404 of 1155 total upregulated genes are upregulated in more than one mutant). Heterochromatin factors and H3K9 methylation are enriched at upregulated genes but not downregulated genes (except let-418).
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis (Figure 3—source data 3) and ChIP-seq enrichment analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). The enrichment analysis appropriately uses peak overlap and fold-change thresholds. The exception for let-418 is appropriately noted.

results.result: In C. elegans, H3K9me2 and H3K9me3 are found in small domains on distal arm regions of autosomes. MET-2 carries out mono- and di-methylation of H3K9, SET-25 primarily carries out tri-methylation, and in the absence of both, H3K9 methylation is undetectable.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 are supported by citations to prior work (Liu et al., 2011; Towbin et al., 2012) and confirmed by the ChIP-seq data in this study (Figure 2A). This represents established knowledge that provides important context for the current findings.

results.result: HP1 contains a chromodomain that binds methylated H3K9. HPL-2 and LIN-61 can bind all methylated forms of H3K9 in vitro, and a complex containing LIN-13, HPL-2, and LIN-61 has been detected in vivo. LET-418 is an ortholog of Mi-2, a nucleosome remodeling component of repressive complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C14 are supported by citations to prior work and represent established knowledge about these factors. This background information is important for interpreting the current findings but does not constitute new results from this study.

results.result: let-418 and lin-13 null mutants are sterile, hpl-2 mutants show temperature-sensitive sterility, and lin-61 and met-2 mutants have slightly reduced brood sizes. hpl-2 mutants produce abnormal oocytes, suggesting defective gametogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C18 are supported by citations to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1. This represents established phenotypic characterization that motivates the current study.

results.result: Prior studies in other organisms have implicated orthologs of these heterochromatin factors in repetitive element regulation. HPL-2 binding in C. elegans embryos was previously shown to be on distal arm regions, SETDB1 binds near endogenous retroviruses in mammalian ES cells, and retrotransposons are derepressed in Setdb1 knockout mice and regulated by HP1α/β in mESCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work. This background information provides important context for the current findings but represents prior knowledge rather than new results.

results.result: The piRNA pathway in C. elegans involves 21nt piRNAs binding PRG-1, triggering secondary 22G siRNAs that mediate silencing in cytoplasm or nucleus. The nuclear RNAi pathway orchestrates H3K9 and H3K27 methylation and/or RNA Pol II inhibition. Regions upregulated in hrde-1 mutants are enriched for retrotransposons.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 are supported by citations to prior work and represent established knowledge about small RNA pathways in C. elegans. This background is essential for understanding the connections to heterochromatin factors but does not constitute new findings.

results.result: One fourth of genes contain a repetitive element bound by a heterochromatin factor, and of those, 59% (3287/5568) are expressed in the germ line.
results.evaluation: Claims C94 and C95 are supported by calculations from ChIP-seq and gene expression data. This observation supports the speculation about local mechanisms of regulation (C93) but is a relatively straightforward descriptive statistic.

results.result: Functional redundancy among factors and pathways underlies the importance of safeguarding the genome through multiple means.
results.evaluation: Claim C92 is a general conclusion supported by the extensive genetic interaction data throughout the manuscript. This represents an appropriate synthesis of the findings but is more of an interpretive statement than a specific result.

results.result: The widespread binding sites and desilencing of additional targets relative to prg-1 indicate that heterochromatin proteins also mediate repression that is not piRNA-induced.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 is a reasonable inference based on the comparison of binding sites and upregulated elements between heterochromatin mutants and prg-1 mutants. The logic is sound, though the conclusion is somewhat speculative about mechanism.

results.result: Heterochromatin factors may act locally within euchromatic domains rather than forming large heterochromatin domains, based on observations that factor binding is closely associated with repeats and genes containing bound repeats are often expressed.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 is explicitly labeled as speculation by the authors. While the observations supporting this speculation (C94, C95) are documented, the claim about local versus spreading mechanisms requires additional experimental evidence such as chromatin conformation studies or higher-resolution binding analyses.

results.result: Heterochromatin factors act to combat different types of genotoxic insults, both through silencing repetitive elements and facilitating repair.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 is a conclusion based on the MIRAGE1 RNAi, spo-11 RNAi, and DNA repair defect data (Figures 4 and 5). This represents a reasonable synthesis of multiple lines of evidence, though the mechanisms of how these factors facilitate repair remain to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Quality control mechanisms in heterochromatin mutant germ lines largely prevent improperly repaired meiotic germ cells from becoming mature gametes, either through apoptosis or arrest of gametogenesis, to ensure low mutation rates.
results.evaluation: Claim C98 is explicitly labeled as a proposal by the authors and is based on the observation that heterochromatin mutants do not show high embryo lethality or visible mutant phenotypes despite DNA damage. While this is a reasonable hypothesis, it requires additional experimental evidence such as direct measurement of mutation rates in progeny or analysis of checkpoint activation.

results.result: C. elegans heterochromatin proteins HPL-2/HP1, LIN-13, LIN-61, LET-418/Mi-2, and MET-2/SETDB1 act together with the piRNA and nuclear RNAi pathways to silence repetitive elements and prevent genotoxic stress in the germ line.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is the main conclusion of the manuscript and is supported by the comprehensive set of results including genetic interactions, ChIP-seq showing co-binding at repeats, RNA-seq showing repeat derepression, connections to piRNA and nuclear RNAi pathways, DNA repair defects, and rescue experiments. This represents an appropriate synthesis of all major findings.

results.result: Heterochromatin is less transcriptionally active than euchromatin and highly enriched for repetitive elements such as transposons and satellite repeats.
results.evaluation: Claim C6 represents established scientific knowledge about heterochromatin properties and provides essential background context. This is appropriately cited as general knowledge.
